question.text: A client in the Young Family stage has Rs.8,00,000 annual income. His annual outflows are: loan EMIs Rs.2,00,000, essential living expenses Rs.3,00,000, and discretionary expenses Rs.1,50,000. After meeting ALL of these listed expense categories (mandatory loan EMIs, essential living expenses, AND discretionary expenses) - i.e., without redirecting any of the discretionary spending - what annual amount is left for savings and investment?

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series XVII workbook pp.65-67, the budgeting framework deducts mandatory expenses first, then essential living, then discretionary expenses; what remains is available for savings and investment. Applying that order to the stem (which expressly says all listed expense categories - including discretionary - are met): Rs.8,00,000 - Rs.2,00,000 (EMIs) - Rs.3,00,000 (essential) - Rs.1,50,000 (discretionary) = Rs.1,50,000. The Trap: Rs.3,00,000 is what one would get by treating discretionary spend as fully redirected to savings - this was the alternative reading the audit flagged as defensible under a "maximum savings" interpretation. Rs.5,00,000 ignores discretionary spending only partially. Rs.8,00,000 ignores all expenses. The stem now expressly bars the "redirect discretionary to savings" reading by stating that all listed expense categories are met without redirecting any discretionary spend. Note: The original stem asked for the "maximum amount available for savings and investment", which under the workbook's own language ("discretionary expenses are last and can be cut back or eliminated to reach required savings") also supported Rs.3,00,000. The stem has been narrowed to ask the amount left after meeting all listed expense categories (without redirecting discretionary), which makes Rs.1,50,000 the uniquely correct answer (NISM Series XVII pp.65-67).
